title: Prussian blue analogue derived dual Ni–N  x  /Fe–N  x   sites coupled with graphitic carbon encapsulated Ni–Fe nanoparticles for selective CO 2  to CO electroreduction
content: Global decarbonization is limited by the absence of low-cost catalysts that combine high selectivity, fast kinetics, and durability. Metal nitrogen carbon (M–N–C) single-atom catalysts have attracted attention, but the mechanistic roles of bimetallic coordination, carbon support architecture, nitrogen doping, and subsurface metallic nanoparticles remain unresolved. Herein, a Prussian Blue Analogue derived electrocatalyst, Ni/Fe–NC, in which surface Ni–Nx/Fe–Nx dual-coordination active sites are proposed to be electronically modulated by graphitically encapsulated Ni–Fe nanoparticle alloy cores distributed on an XC-72R carbon support has been synthesized. The Prussian Blue Analogue precursor enforces crystal lattice level bimetallic pre-organization of Ni and Fe prior to pyrolysis. Through a four-catalyst ablation study, Ni/Fe–NC, Fe–NC, Ni/Fe–C, and Ni/Fe–N, the role of each structural component is examined. X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopic characterization supports the proposed hybrid structural model. Graphitic carbon shells simultaneously suppress the hydrogen evolution reaction, consistent with physical blocking of the HER active metallic surface and are proposed to electronically modulate the overlying metal nitrogen (M–Nx) active sites through the graphene interlayer. Ni/Fe–NC achieves a peak faradaic efficiency for CO of 84.98% at −1.2V vs. Ag/AgCl in CO2 saturated 0.5 M KHCO3, an 8 h average FECO of 78.8%, and the lowest Tafel slope (184 mV dec−1) and an H2 partial current density 8–22 times lower than the three control catalysts. This work proposes graphitic nanoparticle encapsulation as an electronic promotion design lever and provides a transferable Prussian Blue Analogue derived synthetic framework for bimetallic M–N–C electrocatalysts for selective CO2 electroreduction.
